plasma-cell.def: A fully differentiated B cell, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, that releases large amounts of one antibody. Activation needs helper T cell help for T cell-dependent (protein) antigens but not for T cell-independent antigens such as repeating capsule sugars.

antibody-structure.def: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. The variable regions at the arm tips form two antigen-binding sites; the constant regions, including the Fc region of the stem, set the class and bind Fc receptor proteins and complement.

antibody-classes.def: The five kinds of antibody, set by the heavy chain: IgG (main blood antibody, crosses to the fetus), IgA (in secretions), IgM (first made, a pentamer), IgE (on mast cells) and IgD (on naïve B cells). Class switching changes a B cell's class while keeping its variable region.

antibody-actions.def: The ways antibodies disable antigens: neutralization (blocking toxins and viruses from binding cells), agglutination (clumping), opsonization (coating for phagocytes), complement activation and directing natural killer cells. The antibody binds; other cells and proteins do the killing.

primary-secondary-response.def: The primary response to a first exposure has a lag of about 5–10 days and a low peak, mostly IgM then IgG. The secondary response to a later exposure comes from memory cells: faster, much higher, mostly IgG and better fitting. Seroconversion is when antibody first becomes detectable in the blood.

active-passive.def: Active immunity is made by your own immune system, after infection or a vaccine; it is slow to start, leaves memory and lasts long. Passive immunity is borrowed antibody, from mother to baby or by injection; it works at once but fades in weeks to months.

pathogen-responses.def: A pathogen is a microbe or parasite that can cause disease. Each type meets the defenses that can reach it: antibodies and complement for bacteria outside cells, Th1 cells and macrophages for bacteria inside cells, interferons, NK cells, antibodies and cytotoxic T cells for viruses, and Th2 cells, IgE and eosinophils for worms. Immune evasion is a pathogen's ways around them.
